Question: Can you define, deploy, and manage a heterogeneous team of specialised agents with distinct roles, capabilities, and model assignments working toward a shared goal?
Response: Yes. WPP gets the outcome of a heterogeneous team — specialised capabilities with distinct roles, allowed tools and model assignments working toward a shared goal — but achieved through skill-based specialisation inside domain-scoped Hosted Agents plus typed executors inside a MAF workflow graph, not through separate agent processes per role. Execution substrate: Azure Durable Functions is the durable envelope around the whole workflow. Inside each phase, a Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow v1.0 graph wires typed executors — plain-function executors, agent executors, validator executors — with conditional routing, fan-out/fan-in, Pregel BSP execution, and native HITL pause/resume. The DF↔MAF integration uses Microsoft's productised MAF Durable Task extension for Azure Functions (the "Durable Agent Orchestration" pattern, Feb 2026). Where a MAF node is an agent executor, it invokes a GHCP SDK session that loads the role-appropriate skill and tool allow-list with its own model assignment (a screening skill may use a cheap model; a candidate evaluation skill a frontier model). The outcome is a heterogeneous team — distinct roles, tools, models, judges/validators — but with meaningful advantages: no inter-agent communication overhead on the hot path, shared typed state on the MAF graph edges rather than ad-hoc message passing, simpler governance (one Entra identity per domain Hosted Agent), and easier operationalisation at fleet scale. MAF also exposes stable orchestration patterns (sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, Magentic-One) when a true multi-agent topology is required inside a phase. Question: What orchestration topologies are supported: sequential, parallel, hierarchical, peer-to-peer, hybrid? Can the orchestrator select pattern dynamically based on task structure?
Response: All topologies are supported across the two orchestration layers. Between phases, Durable Functions provides sequential flow, fan-out/fan-in, conditional branching and timer-driven escalation. Within a phase, a MAF workflow graph expresses the topology explicitly as typed executors and edges — sequential, parallel (Pregel BSP fan-out/fan-in), hierarchical (a parent executor dispatches to child executors), and MAF's stable multi-agent patterns (sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat, Magentic-One) when multiple agent executors collaborate. Hybrid: DF coordinates between phases while MAF graphs shape execution within. Dynamic selection: an agent executor can reason about next steps and emit a typed result that routes along conditional edges; a planning MAF workflow can select which sub-graph to invoke. Example: if budget approval is pending, sourcing can start in parallel; if a compliance validator fails, the graph routes to a sequential review branch. This is not a static DAG — routing adapts based on runtime data and validator outcomes. Note: Foundry Hosted Agents provide the agent runtime (ephemeral GHCP SDK session container, Responses API surface), while Durable Functions provides the durable envelope for multi-day/multi-week workflows. Hosted Agents alone cannot wait weeks at zero compute for an external event; DF can. Microsoft's Durable Agent Orchestration pattern composes both — this is what WPP's 8-12 week workflows require, not an either/or choice.
Key Technologies: Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) v1.0 workflows (Pregel BSP, sequential/concurrent/handoff/group-chat/Magentic-One), MAF Durable Task extension, Foundry Hosted Agents (runtime), Azure Durable Functions (envelope — fan-out/fan-in, conditional, timer), GHCP SDK agent executors (dynamic reasoning)

Question: Can agents spawn new sub-agents at runtime? Distinguish persistent (registry-stored, governance-reviewed) vs ephemeral (garbage-collected post-task).
Response: Our architecture natively distinguishes persistent and ephemeral execution. Persistent: skills and MAF workflow graphs registered in Azure API Center with lifecycle governance (Design → Preview → Production). These are the governed, reviewed capabilities that agent executors load; a new skill (or a new executor subgraph) can be authored and promoted through the API Center lifecycle — this is the "persistent agent" equivalent. Ephemeral: every GHCP SDK session inside a MAF agent executor is ephemeral by design — it spins up for the executor node, loads skills and tools (with skill-specific tool allow-lists enforced at APIM, not arbitrary MCP tools), reasons, writes typed output, emits OTEL telemetry, and exits. Skill specialisation is preserved: a screening skill loads screening tools; a compensation skill loads compensation tools — this is why we don't need separate agent processes per role. Runtime agent assembly (§6.2): MAF supports dynamic executor creation; spawned persistent agents auto-register in Entra Agent ID (new first-class agent identity for RBAC and audit isolation) and Azure API Center (skill in Design state) via a governance-gate callback, with the spawning decision written to the audit ledger. The spawned agent runs in Design state until a human operator promotes it to Production — no runtime escape from governance. MAF workflows themselves can fan out dynamically (Pregel BSP fan-out/fan-in) to parallel agent executors — e.g. 50 CVs screened in parallel ephemeral sessions. Durable Functions coordinates across phase boundaries. All ephemeral sessions are garbage-collected after completion; state persists in the workflow state store and in MAF's own checkpoints (preserved across DF replay via the Durable Task extension), not in the session.
Key Technologies: GHCP SDK ephemeral sessions, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph (Pregel BSP fan-out), MAF Durable Task extension, Azure API Center (persistent skill registry), Azure Durable Functions fan-out

Question: As workflows stabilise, can orchestration transition from generative (LLM-driven) to deterministic (codified DAGs)? Describe the crystallisation mechanism and version control.
Response: Yes — crystallisation is a core architectural principle and is expressed structurally as a migration within the MAF workflow graph: agent executor → deterministic plain-function executor, with the agent executor preserved as a low-confidence fallback. Skills are the crystallisation artefact. Pattern: (1) Observation — an agent executor reasons through a task using LLM-driven logic (e.g. CV parsing) with a downstream validator executor asserting structural/policy constraints. (2) Validation — after N successful executions where the validator passes and human overrides are rare, the pattern is statistically validated. (3) Code generation — the proven logic is extracted into a deterministic plain-function executor. (4) Review — human reviews the implementation. (5) Promotion — the crystallised skill is registered in Azure API Center and promoted through Design → Preview → Production. (6) Graph swap — the MAF workflow graph is updated: the agent node is replaced by the deterministic function node on the happy path, and an edge routes low-confidence cases back to the agent executor fallback. Result: faster, cheaper, more predictable execution, with graceful fallback for novel input. Version control: SKILL.md files and MAF workflow definitions are Git-committed, synced to API Center, immutable once promoted, and managed through APIOps CI/CD with approval gates.
Key Technologies: Skill crystallisation pipeline, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph (agent → plain-function executor migration), Azure API Center lifecycle, Git version control, APIOps CI/CD approval gates

Question: Describe plan-and-execute cost optimisation: tiered model usage (planner vs executor), token budgets, caching, batching, structured outputs.
Response: Cost optimisation is architectural. (1) Tiered model usage: skills specify the appropriate model tier. Keyword filtering and triage use a cheap fast model. Top-30 candidate evaluation uses a frontier model. Budget checks use structured output with a small model. The skill author selects the model; APIM enforces it. (2) Token budgets: APIM AI Gateway enforces per-agent, per-model token rate limits. Skills can declare token budget expectations. (3) Caching: APIM provides semantic caching for repeated similar queries — identical invoice validation queries hit cache instead of model. (4) Batching: MAF workflow Pregel BSP fan-out enables batch processing — 50 invoices processed in parallel agent executor nodes rather than sequentially, with DF coordinating across phases. (5) Structured outputs: GHCP SDK supports schema-validated responses — the model outputs structured JSON matching a defined schema, reducing token waste and post-processing; MAF typed edges enforce structure between executors; APIM validates every response against the declared schema before propagation and rejects schema violations at the gateway (surfaced to Fleet Manager as quality signals for further crystallisation). (6) Crystallisation: deterministic plain-function executors in the MAF graph bypass the LLM entirely — proven patterns execute as code at near-zero inference cost, with the agent executor preserved as a fallback on low confidence. Cost visibility: OTEL telemetry + APIM metrics provide per-workflow, per-phase cost attribution visible on the Control Plane.
Key Technologies: APIM semantic caching and token limits, tiered Foundry models, GHCP SDK structured outputs, Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) workflow graph (typed edges, BSP fan-out, agent → plain-function executor crystallisation)
